commentary.bottom_line: Forty-one studies used or examined annotator-based reference standards, but most were offline, level 4 reports of rater agreement rather than tests of whether independent, blinded, adjudicated annotation changes accuracy estimates. One prospective deployment study and several adjudication studies suggest the practice may find and correct reference-label errors that single-pass annotation misses.

perspectives.view: One level 2 prospective study found and corrected 102 misdiagnosed slides in a 1,161-slide dataset. The remaining tests are level 4 and offline, and most report agreement (kappa 0.68 to 0.98) without comparing adjudicated and unadjudicated standards. Two records appear to describe the same 426-pair study. Indirectness and inconsistent agreement limit certainty to low.

Hazard studies show that flawed labels distort performance. Models trained on Sepsis-3 labels lost up to 18 AUROC points, and model segmentations outscored reference annotations. Adjudicators found errors that first-pass annotators missed, and structured readjudication overturned 10 of 25 initial CRC discordances. Adjudicators also disagreed with each other, so the practice may catch some errors but not all.

Defined procedures may matter for reliability. A structured workbook raised AGREE II ICCs from -0.09 to 0.66 before to 0.84 to 0.92 after, while reference answers moved Fleiss' kappa only from 0.08 to 0.13. Ten clinicians adjudicating flagged documentation items agreed on genuine errors 59% of the time, and a pilot rubric showed uneven category reliability.

Pairwise raters reached consensus in 60.6% of evaluations, so about four in ten cases needed a third reviewer. Substituting AI judges to reduce this cost may not hold up. AI judges reached an ICC of 0.538 against 0.860 for human experts, and ChatGPT-expert correlation was negligible (tau 0.153).

Clinician graders in a safety-net sample varied widely in sensitivity (0.33 to 0.99), which suggests single-grader labels may be unstable for these patients. Bilingual clinicians rating translated discharge instructions agreed only slightly to moderately (kappa -0.11 to 0.49). No test of the practice was conducted in a US safety-net or limited English proficiency population.

FDA draft guidance asks sponsors to describe annotator training, instructions, and whether annotators were blinded to each other. A regulatory discussion paper expects scoring rubrics to be grounded in clinical guidelines or validated by qualified experts. These are documentation expectations, and the supplied studies do not show which procedures meet them.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared accuracy estimates for the same AI tool when it was scored against an independent, blinded, adjudicated reference standard versus a single-annotator or unblinded standard. Evaluators also lack data on the reviewer time and cost of adjudication in routine health-system evaluations, and on how often corrected labels change deployment decisions.
commentary.underserved_note: Four tests were set in non-English-language settings (Portugal, Switzerland, Sweden, China), but none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patient populations in the United States. A hazard study in a safety-net sample found wide grader variability, so health systems serving these groups cannot assume that published reference-standard procedures yield reliable labels for their patients.
